I was wondering what are the steps to perform factoring kriging. I know it is used to extract specific components that may have a physical meaning and this is achieved by kriging. However, I have some questions regarding the specifics of such procedure. By the way, the following description of the problem belongs to Wackernagel's excellent book Multivariate Geostatistics.

Suppose we have a random variable $Z({\\bf{x}})$ that can be decomposed into some stationary components $Z_{u}({\\bf{x}_{\\alpha}})$ and an intrinsic component $Z_{S}({\\bf{x_{\\alpha}}})$. We are interested in kriging this intrinsic component: $Z_{S}^{*}({\\bf{x_{0}}}) = \\sum_{\\alpha=1}^{n}w_{\\alpha}^{S}Z({\\bf{x_{\\alpha}}})$

Therefore, estimating the variance $\\sigma_{E}^{2}$ we get:

\\begin{array}{} \\sigma_{E}^{2} &= var(Z_{S}^{*}({\\bf{x_{0}}})-Z_{S}({\\bf{x_{0}}}))\\\\ & = \\sum_{u=0}^{S-1}C^{u}({\\bf{x_0}}-{\\bf{x_0}}) - \\gamma^{S}({\\bf{x_0}}-{\\bf{x_0}}) - \\sum_{\\alpha=1}^{n}\\sum_{\\beta=1}^{n}w_{\\alpha}^{S}w_{\\beta}^{S}\\gamma({\\bf{x_\\alpha}}-{\\bf{x_\\beta}})\\\\ &+2\\sum_{\\alpha=1}^{n}w_{\\alpha}^{S}\\gamma^{S}({\\bf{x_\\alpha}}-{\\bf{x_0}}) \\end{array}

and minimizing (with respect to the weights) we obtain:

$$\\sum_{\\beta=1}^{n} w_{\\beta}^{S}\\gamma({\\bf{x_\\alpha}}-{\\bf{x_\\beta}}) + \\mu_{S} = \\gamma^{S}({\\bf{x_\\alpha}}-{\\bf{x_0}}) \\thinspace \\thinspace \\text{for $\\alpha$=1,...n}$$

$$\\sum_{\\beta=1}^{n}w_{\\beta}^{S}=1$$

where $\\mu_{S}$ is the Lagrange multiplier due to the constraint on the weights.

As I understand it, the idea usually is to get the weights $w_{\\beta}$ that minimize the variance $\\sigma_{E}^{2}$ in order to estimate new values ${\\bf{x_{0}}}$. The most important downside for searching along single parameters instead of optimizing them all together is that you ignore interactions. It is quite common that e.g. more than one parameter influences model complexity. In that case, you need to look at the interaction in order to sucessfully optimize the hyperparameters.

Depending on how large your data set is and how many models you compare, optimization strategies that return the maximum observed performance run into trouble (true for both grid search and your strategy). The reason is that searching through a large number of performance estimates for the maximum "skims" the variance of the performance estimate: you may just end up with a model and train/test split combination that accidentally happens to look good. Even worse, you may get several perfect looking combinations, and the optimization then cannot know which model to choose and thus becomes unstable.
It's better to use all available data. If your data is unbalanced, then it's not cool to remove the data to make the panel balanced. Instead, you apply methods which handle unbalanced panels.

rows: Well, the [gee][1] package includes facilities for fitting GEE and `gee()` return asymptotic and robust SE. I never used the [geepack][2] package. From what I saw in the online example, output seems to resemble more or less that of `gee`. To compute $100(1-\\alpha)$ CIs for your main effects (e.g. gender), why not use the robust SE (in the following I will assume it is extracted from, say `summary(gee.fit)`, and stored in a variable `rob.se`)? I suppose that\\n\\n    exp(coef(gee.fit)["gender"]+c(-1,1)*rob.se*qnorm(0.975))\\n\\nshould yield 95% CIs expressed on the odds scale.\\n\\nNow, in fact I rarely use GEE except when I am working with binary endpoints in longitudinal studies, because it's easy to pass or estimate a given working correlation matrix. In the case you summarize here, I would rather rely on an IRT model for dichotomous items (see the [psychometrics][3] task view), or (it is quite the same in fact) a mixed-effects GLM such as the one that is proposed in the [lme4][4] package, from Doug Bates. For study like yours, as you said, subjects will be considered as random effects, and your other covariates enter the model as fixed effects; the response is the 0/1 rating on each item (which enter the model as well). Then you will get 95% CI for fixed effects, either from the SE computed as `sqrt(diag(vcov(glmm.fit)))` or as read in `summary(glmm.fit)`, or using `confint()` together with an `lmList` object. Doug Bates gave nice illustrations in the following two paper/handout:\\n\\n* [Estimating the Multilevel Rasch Model: With the lme4 Package][5] (JSS, 2007 20(2))\\n* [Item Response Models as GLMMs][6] (from a workshop at UseR 2008)\\n\\nThere is also a discussion about profiling `lmer` fits (based on *profile deviance*) to investigate variability in fixed effects, but I didn't investigate that point. I think it is still in section 1.5 of Doug's [draft on mixed models][7]. Well, the gee package includes facilities for fitting GEE and gee() return asymptotic and robust SE. I never used the geepack package. From what I saw in the online example, output seems to resemble more or less that of gee. To compute $100(1-\\alpha)$ CIs for your main effects (e.g. gender), why not use the robust SE (in the following I will assume it is extracted from, say summary(gee.fit), and stored in a variable rob.se)? I suppose that

exp(coef(gee.fit)["gender"]+c(-1,1)*rob.se*qnorm(0.975))

should yield 95% CIs expressed on the odds scale.

Now, in fact I rarely use GEE except when I am working with binary endpoints in longitudinal studies, because it's easy to pass or estimate a given working correlation matrix. In the case you summarize here, I would rather rely on an IRT model for dichotomous items (see the psychometrics task view), or (it is quite the same in fact) a mixed-effects GLM such as the one that is proposed in the lme4 package, from Doug Bates. For study like yours, as you said, subjects will be considered as random effects, and your other covariates enter the model as fixed effects; the response is the 0/1 rating on each item (which enter the model as well). Then you will get 95% CI for fixed effects, either from the SE computed as sqrt(diag(vcov(glmm.fit))) or as read in summary(glmm.fit), or using confint() together with an lmList object. Doug Bates gave nice illustrations in the following two paper/handout:

  • Estimating the Multilevel Rasch Model: With the lme4 Package (JSS, 2007 20(2))
  • Item Response Models as GLMMs (from a workshop at UseR 2008)

There is also a discussion about profiling lmer fits (based on profile deviance) to investigate variability in fixed effects, but I didn't investigate that point. I think it is still in section 1.5 of Doug's draft on mixed models. There are a lot of discussion about computing SE and CI for GLMM as implemented in the lme4 package (whose interface differs from the previous nlme package), so that you will easily find other interesting threads after googling about that.

It's not clear to me why GEE would have to be preferred in this particular case. Maybe, look at the R translation of Agresti's book by Laura Thompson, R (and S-PLUS) Manual to Accompany Agresti's Categorical Data.

I want to check if a new equipment improves a score compared with the older equipment. My database contains the score with the old equipment, and the scores with each new equipment. I googled, userR'd, checked similar journal articles and saw that one of them used the sign test to assess the improvement in the grading.

EDIT

To make it clear, the journal article which studied a very similar question used the sign test. They and I have data like this one:

               New equipment
Old equipment  1  2  3
            1 33  0  0
            2 37  8  1
            3 12  4  0
            4  2  0  0

This table should be read like this:

  • Numbers 1-4 are scores for some condition (1 is better, 4 is worst).

  • The first row starting with 1 means that the old equipment provided a score of 1 in 33 patients, and the situation did not change with the new equipment.

  • The second row starting with 2 means that the old equipment provided a score of 2 in 46 patients (derived from 37+8+1). The new equipment provided a score of 3 in 1 patient, a score of 2 in 8 patients, and a score of 1 in 37 patients. This is a good improvement, but in ~2% of cases, things may get worse.

  • The third row starting with 3 means that the old equipment provided a score of 3 in 16 patients (derived from 12+4). The new equipment provided a score of 2 in 4 patients, and a score of 1 in 12 patients. This is a major improvement.

  • The fourth row starting with 4 means that the old equipment provided a score of 4 in 2 patients. The new equipment provided a score of 1 in both of these patients. This is a major improvement. However, only 2 out of 97 patients scored 4 with no instrument. Therefore we may conclude that only patients who score high (3 or 4) with no instrument may benefit from using an instrument.

I think that the best option is to test each row separately with wilcoxon test, by comparing the medians of both conditions (old equipment and new equipment). As an example:

score.2 <- subset(original.df, old-equipment %in% 2)
wilcox.test(score.2$old-equipment, score.2$new-equipment, alternative="great")

and repeat this for each score with the old equipment. I couldn't see a way to use the sign test for this. What is your suggestion to test this condition properly?

EDIT#2

I think the Wilcoxon signed rank test is appropriate to compare the differences of two new methods/instruments over a common old method/instrument. But when it comes to test the significance of the difference of one method over the other, it has a shortcoming. Let me explain with an example:

Lets say, on 4 trials, I could eat 3,4,4,5 peas with a fork. With a spoon, I could eat 4,5,5,6 peas. Since the median of the spoon-trial is higher than the median of the fork-trial, we can conclude that spoon is better for eating peas. It won't differ if the spoon-trial ends up as 6,5,5,4 or 5,5,5,5 or even 1,1,10,10. The spoon-median is higher than the fork-median and the Wilcoxon test will yield a low p-value. But when it comes to grading or notes, or anything that requires consistency, it differs. In my case, I'm working with old and new scoring systems. When a new method/instrument consistently achieves higher scores compared with the old one, it is simply better than the old one. But when it achieves very good scores in half of the trials, and very bad scores in the other half (but still better sum or median than the old one), it is not better. It may score better in some circumstances but it is not reliable. That is the weakness of the Wilcoxon test. It does not take the paired nature of the data into account.

So my exact question is, how can I make the Wilcoxon test see this problem from a "paired samples" aspect. So I have data, where I test each subject with three different instruments and would like to know if it is worth the effort to switch to any of the new instruments.
